implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent ships both halves and the CyclicBarrier javadoc's own matrix-decomposition example is the canonical usage: CyclicBarrier(N) trips when all N parties call await(), the optional Runnable runs once per generation inside the last arriving thread (the aggregation hook), await() returns the arrival index so a chosen thread can do phase-local work, and the barrier re-arms itself for the next phase. CountDownLatch is the one-shot gate - countDown() from N producers, await() or await(timeout) in the collector - and it cannot be reset, so a second round needs a new instance. Interruption, timeout or reset breaks the whole barrier all-or-none, surfacing BrokenBarrierException to every waiter.
pitfalls: The all-or-none breakage model: if one thread is interrupted, times out or the barrier action throws, every waiting thread gets BrokenBarrierException and the barrier stays broken until reset() - catch it and abort deliberately instead of retrying inside the worker loop.

CountDownLatch is one-shot: awaiting it twice without re-arming always returns immediately after the first release, and countDown() called more often than N is harmless but signals nothing extra - the counts are not symmetric.
A latch awaited on the same bounded pool that runs the producers deadlocks under saturation; use a separate collector thread or a timeout that detects the stall.
A CyclicBarrier action runs in the last arriver's thread and its exception is propagated there while breaking the barrier; expensive or blocking work in the action serializes the phase.

variants.name: Phaser (dynamic parties, tiered phases)
variants.implementation_notes: When the party is not fixed, Phaser replaces CyclicBarrier: parties register() (the constructor can pre-register them), arriveAndAwaitAdvance() blocks the current phase, arriveAndDeregister() retires a participant without stranding the others, and overriding onAdvance(phase, registered) decides when the phaser terminates. Phasers also tier, so many parties can be grouped behind a few parents instead of contending on one barriered counter. Choose it when workers join or leave between phases; keep CyclicBarrier when the party size is genuinely fixed, because its barrier action and arrival-index API is simpler.
pitfalls: A Phaser is not a latch: awaitAdvance(phase) observes one phase, and there is no built-in timeout on the plain arrive/wait calls - use arriveAndAwaitAdvance interleaved with awaitAdvanceInterruptibly when a bounded wait is required.

Deregistering the last party of a phase advances it for everyone; retiring a worker too early (before its final phase) silently shortens the next phase, and doing it twice throws IllegalStateException.

Once the phaser terminates, arriveAndAwaitAdvance throws IllegalStateException in every remaining party, so the onAdvance termination condition and the workers' exit condition must be the same predicate.

variants.name: CompletableFuture.allOf (non-blocking latch)
variants.idiom_name: CompletableFuture.allOf(...).thenRun(...) instead of a blocking latch
variants.implementation_notes: When the completions are already futures, the latch becomes composition instead of blocking: allOf(futures) yields a future that completes only when every input completed (exceptionally if any did), thenRun/thenApply chains the continuation without parking a thread, and the fan-in can be bounded with orTimeout or completeOnTimeout. On Java 21+ the same shape composes with virtual threads, so a blocking-style body per task is cheap while the collector still never blocks a platform thread. Keep the classic primitives when threads must rendezvous for a phase; use this form when the pattern is purely 'proceed after N completions'.
pitfalls: allOf completes only after every input future completes; if any input failed the result is exceptional, but the other futures keep running: cancel them or bound the pool, otherwise a failed fan-in leaks work.

join() on the calling thread is still a blocking wait - calling it on a pool thread that the futures themselves need deadlocks; prefer continuations (thenRun/thenApply) and keep join for the boundary.
orTimeout/completeOnTimeout mutate the future and exist from Java 9; on Java 8 the timeout must be enforced by the caller, and a timed-out allOf leaves its inputs running.
